query: I need SAME-TEST seawater corrosion data that compare unalloyed copper (or a copper alloy with less than 5 wt% Ni) against 90-10 copper-nickel (C70600) and/or 70-30 copper-nickel (C71500), measured in the same study under the same conditions (natural or synthetic seawater, or 3.5 wt% NaCl; quiet immersion preferred; mass loss or weight loss preferred over Tafel; 30 days or longer preferred). Also any same-study series of Cu-Ni alloys with several Ni contents between 0 and 30 wt% (for example Cu-2Ni, Cu-5Ni, Cu-10Ni, Cu-30Ni), and any same-study comparison of an aluminum bronze (Cu-5Al to Cu-9Al, with or without Fe) against a copper-nickel. For each, give: the paper (authors, year, DOI), each alloy's composition in wt%, product form, the test (medium, temperature, flow, duration, method), and each alloy's corrosion rate exactly as reported with units. List only numbers you can see in the source; say which table or figure each comes from. Prefer peer-reviewed papers and authoritative compilations (for example LaQue, Efird, the Copper Development Association, INCO/Nickel Institute), and say which are compilations.
task_summary: Same Test Seawater Corrosion Data Comparing Copper And Copper‑Nickel Alloys With Experimental Details

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2

        - PHASE4: Phase 4

    StandardAge:

        - COMPLETED: Study completed

        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting

        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: I need SAME-TEST seawater corrosion data that compare unalloyed copper (or a copper alloy with less than 5 wt% Ni) against 90-10 copper-nickel (C70600) and/or 70-30 copper-nickel (C71500), measured in the same study under the same conditions (natural or synthetic seawater, or 3.5 wt% NaCl; quiet immersion preferred; mass loss or weight loss preferred over Tafel; 30 days or longer preferred). Also any same-study series of Cu-Ni alloys with several Ni contents between 0 and 30 wt% (for example Cu-2Ni, Cu-5Ni, Cu-10Ni, Cu-30Ni), and any same-study comparison of an aluminum bronze (Cu-5Al to Cu-9Al, with or without Fe) against a copper-nickel. For each, give: the paper (authors, year, DOI), each alloy's composition in wt%, product form, the test (medium, temperature, flow, duration, method), and each alloy's corrosion rate exactly as reported with units. List only numbers you can see in the source; say which table or figure each comes from. Abstract:
The suitability of copper nickel alloys for use in components of Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) systems is examined by scrutiny of data from appropriate tests and records in related applications. Copper-nickel alloy C70600 is found to exhibit excellent corrosion resistance against seawater flow rates up to 3.0 m/s. The copper-nickels are found to be galvanically compatible as a family and with other copper-base alloys in seawater. Their corrosion rate is found not to be significantly influenced by ambient variations in oxygen content, temperature, or other parameters which change with depth. Low level chlorination does not adversely affect these alloys. Adverse effects of sulfide are not anticipated. The copper-nickel alloys have excellent resistance to macrobiological fouling in seawater, but microfouling still occurs to a limited extent. The danger of leakage of ammonia into seawater, and vice versa, is found to effectively remove copper-nickel alloys as candidates for use in OTEC heat exchangers in contact with ammonia as a working fluid. 132 references. Abstract:
Due to its excellent performance, 90-10 cupronickel has been widely used as a pipeline for marine engineering. However, due to the harsh service conditions of flowing seawater, the problem of corrosion leakage is extremely serious. One of the most common locations is the welding joint. In this paper, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, surface morphology analysis techniques (scanning electron spectroscopy, energy disperse spectroscopy, three-dimensional microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy) are used to study the corrosion resistance of 90-10 cupronickel (MZ), heat affected zone (HAZ) and welding zone (WZ). The experimental results show that MZ, HAZ and WZ can form protective corrosion product film in flowing seawater, and that the corrosion resistance increases with the experiment time increasing and achieves the maximum value after 20 days. However, the corrosion resistance of HAZ is smallest due to the low adhesion density of corrosion production formed on HAZ. HAZ is preferentially corroded for minimum corrosion resistance and galvanic corrosion between WZ and HAZ.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Seawater emerges as a promising source of renewable energy that generates electricity by utilizing the conductive properties of saline water. A seawater-lamp-based energy device can produce low-voltage power through electrochemical reactions between dissimilar metal electrodes. Nonetheless, the presence of a complex ionic composition of seawater creates a harsh corrosive environment, hence reducing the electrode’s longevity. Despite increasing interest in seawater batteries, a research gap remains regarding the comparison of the role of chloride concentration on corrosion behaviour in natural seawater versus simplified salt solutions in active electrical circuits. Copper (Cu) and aluminium (Al) electrode pairs, which offer high potential difference and low material costs, were selected to address the lack of studies on accelerated corrosion data for seawater batteries. The aim of this study is to investigate the effects of varying chloride concentrations on electrode corrosion by comparing natural seawater with prepared sodium chloride (NaCl) solutions. Cu-Al electrode pairs were connected to a 2.5 V light bulb and utilized an impressed current. Corrosion rates were determined using the weight-loss method, while the surface characterization of electrode deposition was further determined by optical microscopy, Scanning Electron Microscopy/Energy Dispersive X-ray (SEM/EDX), and Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR). The findings suggest that although seawater yielded higher electrical performance and brightest illumination, it also exhibited rapid deterioration, with Cu and Al exceeding corrosion rates of 40 mm/yr and 8 mm/yr, respectively. Overall, the study suggests that seawater is a viable energy source for the development of low-cost, off-grid lighting due to its abundant availability and low environmental impact.</jats:p>

2.2   Less Important Forms o f Corrosion


           I n the RRGE systems the  f o l l o w i n g forms o f corrosion are thought  t o
be   l e s s important than those discussed   i n Section  2.1.


      2.2.1      Galvanic Corrosion


     Galvanic corrosion   i s the accelerated wastage o f metal due  t o the
galvanic a c t i o n o f two d i s s i m i l a r metals   i n contact.   While both m e t a l l i c
members o f  t h e s t r u c t u r e may be corroded,  the   l e s s  r e s i s t a n t member
shows an increase   i n corrosion  r a t e w h i l e the more  r e s i s t a n t corrodes
 l e s s than  i f  i t alone were exposed  t o the environment,   The more  r e s i s t a n t
member   i s s a i d  t o be cathodic and the   l e s s  r e s i s t a n t member anodic.  The
parameters  t h a t are important   i n galvanic corrosion are the  r e l a t i v e
electrochemical a c t i v i t i e s o f the two metals,  the temperature,  the
r e l a t i v e areas o f the two metals,  and the chemistry o f the environment.


     The p o t e n t i a l differences between various metals   i n geothermal
b r i n e s has n o t been studied.   However,  the  r e l a t i v e ranking o f a numberof alloys   i n sea water (Figure 2.2.1)  has been made and can serve as a
guide in predicting the behavior of these materials  in geothermal  brines
that have been cooled to about 15C (288K) to 25C (29810.  Some galvanic
potentials have been measured.   For example, Brown ('1   studied the
potentials of a number of aluminum alloys  vs.  annealed copper, hard
drawn copper and brass.   While Brown's study was conducted  a t about 2OC
(29310   i n tap and   i n distilled water,  his results indicate  t h a t large
electrochemical potentials can occur between the materials  he studied.


     Temperature effects   i n galvanic corrosion are not unusual;   thus,
as the temperature increases the rate of corrosion also increases.
However, the rate of change of electrochemical  potential  with temp-
erature  i s not the same for a l l metals.   For example,  a t room temp-
erature zinc    i s anodic with respect  t o iron.   As the temperature in-
creases   t h e potentials converge and a t some elevated temperature   t h e
iron may become anodic with respect  t o zinc (11).


     Galvanic corrosion may be combined w i t h other forms of corrosion.
For example,  if the solution    i s in the nearly neutral   t o moderately
basic pH range a coating of Fe(OH)3 forms on the iron and pitting
crevice corrosion can occur.


     Aluminum heat exchanger tubes have been considered for the primary
heat transfer system of the RRGE demonstration plant.   The possibility
t h a t a reaction can take place between the heat exchanger tubes and
copper  t h a t may occur naturally   i n the Raft River geothermal  brine
places a serious limitation on the use of aluminum.  The reaction  is:

           2 A1 + 3 Cu++ = 2 A1+++  + 3 Cu

t o give a deposit of metallic copper on the aluminum tubes.   These
metallic copper deposits would act as galvanic couples and severe
pitting of the aluminum would result.   The effect of temperature  (i.e.,
the chemical kinetics) on the copper-aluminum reaction has been investigated




                                44                ..         1 - _.   I._.
by MacKinnon and Ingraham (30331)in Canada and by Malhotra (32) in the
U.S.   Their work shows that the reaction is controlled by diffusion of
copper ion through a boundary layer at the temperatures of interest in
the RRGE systems.  The effect of bicarbonate ion (present in Raft River
geothermal brines) on this reaction has been reported by Becerra and
Darb~(~~).

     Even when dissimilar metals are in contact, galvanic corrosion may
not occur or may be sufficiently slow that serious trouble or short life
is not a problem.  This can happen because one or both of the metals may
be passivated after a short time.

     The concentration of dissolved solids and the conductivity of the
Raft River geothermal brines are such that they provide a very good
electrolyte for galvanic corrosion.  The possibility of forming dissimilar
metal couples is probably highest in the cooling tower and care must be
exercised to prevent accidental coupling.  Both the hot and cold brine
transmission lines are additional sites for galvanic corrosion and
particular attention must be given to materials selection and procurement
to insure that galvanic corrosion is prevented or controlled.

     Hermannsson (16)  noted that zinc on galvanized iron was severely
attacked in Icelandic geothermal waters containing more than about 1 ppm
dissolved oxygen.  This attack is attributed  t o galvanic corrosion
resulting from the depolarization o f both iron and zinc surfaces.  One
must cbnclude that the propensity for galvanic attack is even greater in
the more saline Raft River geothermal brines.

Specimens in the autoclaves are imbedded in packing.

42 months with intermediate inspections at 1,4,10,18 and 28 months. Support of license applications will

crease with temperature from 150°C to 300*C after both one and four months' exposure. Rates range from

rate drops between one and four months. Similar results were observed with OF copper, rates ranging from
2.45 to 57.57 mm/yr for the range of conditions given above. Corrosion rates for 90-10 copper-nickel were
significantly lower, however, as shown in Table 2.

Abstract:
Copper-based materials have long been used for their outstanding thermal and electrical conductivities in various applications, such as heat exchangers, induction heat coils, cooling channels, radiators, and electronic connectors. The development of advanced copper alloys has broadened their utilization to include structural applications in harsh service conditions found in industries like oil and gas, marine, power plants, and water treatment, where good corrosion resistance and a combination of high strength, wear, and fatigue tolerance are critical. These advanced multi-component structures often have complex designs and intricate geometries, requiring extensive metallurgical processing routes and the joining of the individual components into a final structure. Additive manufacturing (AM) has revolutionized the way complex structures are designed and manufactured. It has reduced the processing steps, assemblies, and tooling while also eliminating the need for joining processes. However, the high thermal conductivity of copper and its high reflectivity to near-infrared radiation present challenges in the production of copper alloys using fusion-based AM processes, especially with Yb-fiber laser-based techniques. To overcome these difficulties, various solutions have been proposed, such as the use of high-power, low-wavelength laser sources, preheating the build chamber, employing low thermal conductivity building platforms, and adding alloying elements or composite particles to the feedstock material. This article systematically reviews different aspects of AM processing of common industrial copper alloys and composites, including copper-chrome, copper-nickel, tin-bronze, nickel-aluminum bronze, copper-carbon composites, copper-ceramic composites, and copper-metal composites. It focuses on the state-of-the-art AM techniques employed for processing different copper-based materials and the associated technological and metallurgical challenges, optimized processing variables, the impact of post-printing heat treatments, the resulting microstructural features, physical properties, mechanical performance, and corrosion response of the AM-fabricated parts. Where applicable, a comprehensive comparison of the results with those of their conventionally fabricated counterparts is provided.

     Studies of aluminum alloys over a l2-month period in 180-2500 F
     sea water show the alloys to be independent of dissolved oxygen

     During 1970, research was initiated by OSW (31, p. 451) to develop
fundamental knowledge concerning the behavior of aluminum in desalination
equipment. These studies were started because of the unexpected galvanic
attack between aluminum alloys in the brine heater of the OSW pilot plant
(built by Reynolds Metals Co.) at Wrightsville Beach, N.C., because of the
excessively rapid dissipation of the cladding on Alclad tubes, and because
of the rapid utilization of aluminum anodes in the hot and evaporator sections.

     Investigators of the Reynolds Metals Co. (35) reported on the electro-
chemical performance of aluminum alloys under distillation desalination plant
water chemistry conditions. Potentiometric testing of several aluminum alloys
revealed that there is considerable instability of potential during the first
few hours of exposure of most aluminum alloys to saline solutions; such
instability of potential could be instrumental to initiating corrosive attack.
Their investigation indicated that alloys containing 0.9 percent or more
magnesium may be subject to serious pitting corrosion problems. Some alloys
have a dual temperature-potential curve. Of the 5,000 series alloys, which
are prime candidates for desalination service, only alloy 5005 had a single
temperature-potential curve.

     Other studies of the Reynolds investigators included alloy composition
solution velocity, weldment performance, cold work on potential, and low-
oxygen content of solutions. Comments on only a few of tHese are included
here:

     At 3000 F and above, copper content had no effect on potentials;
     at lower temperatures there were both positive and negative effects.

     Nei ther iron nor silicon, in quanti ties usually found in aluminum
     alloys, had a significant effect on potentials.

     Zinc caused a negative shift in potential that became less evident
     with increasing temperature.

     They found that alloys of relatively high purity would be desirable
for plant construction because of the effects of alloying constituents and
temperature on corrosion potential; alloys 1235 and 5005 were favored.
They were of the opinion that steady high-temperature operations would not
be a serious problem for aluminum alloys.12


     Laboratory work in which the electrochemical potential behavior of
various aluminum alloys in pilot plant environments of a distillation desalt-
ing process was described by Snodgrass (37). Polarization and transient
voltage measurements were also made. Transient voltage measurements can be
used to detect active pitting on aluminum alloys. Although not fully
developed, such measurements appear to have great utility in studying effects
of parameters such as pH and chloride concentration on corrosion.

                               In Geothermal Media

     Corrosion tes t data on Alcoa 3003 by Foster, Marshall, and Tombs (18)
demonstrated weight gain and internal attack in Wairakei bore water at
2400 C and separated steam at 1930 C and 180 pounds per square inch, gage;
the alloy also exhibited blistering in the bore water. In their stress corro-
sion tests, no macroscopic cracking or microscopic surface fissures were
apparent. Aluminum has been found satisfactory at The Geysers for circulating
water lines (~), aluminum butterfly valves in aluminum pipe risers of cooling
towers, tubes in turbine oil coolers, and as exterior sheathing on buildings.
When exposed to condensate for 150 days at the geothermal field in Hveragerdi,
Iceland, pure aluminum was one of the few materials that showed no visible
corrosion (13).

     Corrosion tests were made on aluminum and several other materials in
geothermal fluids of the Cerro Prieto field. Aluminum (99.9+ percent Al) was
used in tests in separated aerated steam, separated condensed steam at low
velocity, separated condensed steam at high velocity, and in atmospheric
exposure tests (38). The only material of those tested that exhibited corro-
sion resistance superior to aluminum in separated aerated steam was
Stellite 6, a high-cobalt alloy; the only material that exhibited signifi-
cantly superior corrosion resistance in separated condensed steam of low
velocity was an austenitic stainless steel, AISI 304; and the only materials
that exhibited superior corrosion resistance in separated condensed steam of
high velocity were stainless steels AISI 304 and AISI 410. In the atmospheric
exposure tes ts, no material was significantly superior to aluminum.

     Copper and copper-base alloys have a unique combination of properties
that make them an excellent choice for many hot concentrated brine applica-

practically immune to stress corrosion cracking while having good resistance
to general corrosion. Furthermore, copper is the most resistant metal to

a higher valence state, and it may promote formation of a protective film on                                                                                  13


the metal surface. Experiments at 3000 to 3100 F have shown that copper ion
pickup in sea water has been decreased from 23 parts per million before
deaeration to only 0.17 part per million after deaeration.

Abstract:
The effects of aluminum on the mechanical properties and corrosion behavior in artificial seawater of Cu-Ni-Fe-Mn alloys were investigated. Cu-7Ni-xAl-1Fe-1Mn samples, consisting of 0, 1, 3, 5, and 7 wt % aluminum along with the same contents of other alloying elements (Ni, Fe, and Mn), were prepared. The microstructure of Cu-7Ni-xAl-1Fe-1Mn alloy was analyzed by Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), and its corrosion property was tested by an electrochemical system. The results show that the mechanical and corrosion properties of Cu-7Ni-xAl-1Fe-1Mn alloy have an obvious change with the aluminum content. The tensile strength has a peak value of 395 MPa by adding 3 wt % aluminum in the alloy. Moreover, the corrosion rate in artificial seawater of Cu-7Ni-3Al-1Fe-1Mn alloy is 0.0215 mm/a which exhibits a better corrosion resistance than the commercially used UNS C70600. It is confirmed that the second-phase transformation of Cu-7Ni-xAl-1Fe-1Mn alloy follows the sequence of α solid solution → Ni3Al → Ni3Al + NiAl → Ni3Al + NiAl3. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) shows that the adding element aluminum in the Cupronickel can improve the corrosion resistance of Cu-7Ni-xAl-1Fe-1Mn alloy.

Abstract:
The 70/30 copper–nickel alloy is used mainly in critical parts with more demanding conditions in marine settings. There is a need for innovative methods that offer fast production and cost-effectiveness in order to supplement current copper–nickel alloy manufacturing processes. In this study, we employ wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) to fabricate the 70/30 copper–nickel alloy. The as-built microstructure is characterized by columnar grains with prominent dendrites and chemical segregation in the inter-dendritic area. The aspect ratio of the columnar grain increases with increasing travel speed (TS) at the same wire feed speed (WFS). This is in contrast with the equiaxed grain structure, with a more random orientation, of the conventional sample. The sample built with a WFS of 8 m/min, TS of 1000 mm/min, and a track distance of 3.85 mm exhibits superior corrosion properties in the 3.5 wt% NaCl solution when compared with the conventional sample, as evidenced by a higher film resistance and breakdown potential, along with a lower passive current density of the WAAM sample. The corrosion morphology reveals the critical roles played by the nickel element that is unevenly distributed between the dendrite core and inter-dendritic area.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Monel-400, a nickel-copper-based alloy, is renowned for its exceptional corrosion resistance, high strength, and toughness across diverse operating environments. However, these desirable properties also make Monel-400 a challenging material to machine using conventional techniques, leading to excessive tool wear, poor surface finish, and high thermal stresses. There is currently no comprehensive review that systematically consolidates and compares non-conventional machining approaches applied to Monel-400 alloy. This review critically examines the non-conventional machining methods employed to address these challenges, including Electric Discharge Machining (EDM), Wire EDM (WEDM), Electrochemical Machining (ECM), Plasma Arc Cutting (PAC), Abrasive Water Jet Machining (AWJM), Photochemical Machining (PCM), and Hot Machining. A systematic comparison of process performance, surface integrity, material removal rate (MRR), Tool Wear Rate (TWR), Surface Roughness (Ra), and optimization strategies is presented. Key advancements such as hybrid dielectrics, cryogenic treatments, near-dry machining, and AI-based optimization techniques are discussed. Challenges related to surface defects, environmental sustainability, tool degradation, and process scalability are highlighted, along with identified research gaps. Future research directions emphasize the development of eco-friendly machining solutions, hybrid machining systems, real-time adaptive control, and life cycle assessments to enable sustainable industrial applications. This review consolidates fragmented knowledge, provides a roadmap for future innovation, and supports the advancement of efficient, precise, and environmentally responsible machining practices for Monel-400.</jats:p>

A.M. Alfantazi, T.M. Ahmed, and D. Tromans. Corrosion behavior of copper alloys in chloride media. Materials & Design, 30:2425-2430, Aug 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2008.10.015, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2008.10.015. This article has 357 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt describes Alfantazi, Ahmed, and Tromans (2009), which examined copper-alloy electrochemical behavior using potentiodynamic polarization rather than reporting a same-test mass-loss corrosion-rate series. Tests used 1 M NaCl at pH 6.5 and 10, including buffered and unbuffered chloride conditions. The alloys were commercial solid-solution materials with nominal compositions Cu–30Ni, Cu–30Zn, and 90Cu–8Al–2Fe (aluminum bronze); pure copper was also tested as a reference. At pH 6.5, the polarization response showed no evidence of passivity and was dominated by copper. Abstract

   Seawater is inherently chemically aggressive, and therefore, constructional materials used in seawater handling
and processing systems including desalination plants are subjected to varying degree of corrosion depending upon
the nature of the material(s) and operational conditions. Broadly speaking, for applications in seawater, the materials
are usually exposed to three zones, namely, fully immersed, partially immersed or seawater surrounding environment.
Interestingly, from corrosion point of view, the seawater behaves differently under the aforementioned conditions.
A study was undertaken to investigate the effect of seawater level on a number of alloys having wide applications
as structural materials in seawater processing plants. The laboratory immersion test technique has been applied to
evaluate the effect of seawater level on the corrosion behavior of different alloys. In three sets of experiments, carbon
steels (G1010 and 1020), austenitic stainless steels (304 SS and 316L SS), cupro-nickel (90/10 Cu/Ni and 70/30
Cu/Ni), Ni-based alloys (Incoloy 825 and Inconel 625) were utilized. The specimens were fixed at three locations
namely, above seawater surface, semi submerged in seawater and fully submerged in seawater. The experiments were
carried out at room temperature with very slow seawater movement (12 L/h). The exposure time was varied between
1–2 years. In this study the corrosion behavior of different alloys has been evaluated based on exposure location.
Besides corrosion rate calculations, the localized attack has also been discussed on the basis of the magnitude of pit
depths.

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000053

From text 'lewis1981evaluationofcoppernickel pages 48-55'.

R. O. Lewis and F. Laque. Evaluation of copper-nickel alloys for otec applications. ArXiv, Apr 1981. URL: https://doi.org/10.2172/6255887, doi:10.2172/6255887. This article has 5 citations.

The Lewis and LaQue (1981) excerpt provides Table XIV data for uncoupled alloys after one-year exposures in 0.6 m/s flowing seawater, using equal-area galvanic couples. The uncoupled corrosion rate for C70600 copper-nickel alloy was 30.5 µm/y (1.2 mpy), while C71500 was 20.3 µm/y (0.8 mpy). Aluminum bronze had an uncoupled rate of 43.2 µm/y (1.7 mpy), and nickel-aluminum bronze measured 150.0 µm/y (5.9 mpy). Carbon steel and titanium are also listed at 330.0 µm/y (13.0 mpy) and less than 2.5 µm/y (less than 0.1 mpy), respectively. These are measured corrosion-rate results, not alloy composition specifications: the excerpt identifies alloys by UNS designations and does not provide their exact measured weight-percent compositions. The excerpt does not contain the requested Gdowski Table 34/35, Ravindran Table 5, or Banning Oden Tables 7/8 data, so it cannot support exact ocean depth, exposure duration, alloy-form, weighing-method, or composition details from those sources.

From text 'lewis1981evaluationofcoppernickel pages 43-48'.

R. O. Lewis and F. Laque. Evaluation of copper-nickel alloys for otec applications. ArXiv, Apr 1981. URL: https://doi.org/10.2172/6255887, doi:10.2172/6255887. This article has 5 citations.

The excerpt does not contain Gdowski (1991) Tables 34/35, Ravindran (1983) Table 5, Banning Oden (1973) Tables 7/8, or Lewis and LaQue (1981) Table XIV, so it cannot supply the requested exact ocean mass-loss rates, test depths, durations, alloy forms, weight-measurement status, compositions, test methods, or uncoupled one-year rates from those tables. It does include related Lewis and LaQue seawater data. Table III reports low-velocity exposure results for C70600 (90-10 Cu-Ni), C71500 (70-30 Cu-Ni), and C72200, distinguishing quiet seawater from flowing seawater at 2 ft/s and giving corrosion rates in MPY plus pitting depths in mils. Table IV reports C71900 and C71500 after no-flow exposures and 2-ft/s flow; durations are 6–9 months for C71900 and one year for C71500, with corrosion rates in inches per year and localized attack depths in inches. These are measured exposure results, not alloy specification ranges. Table VII separately identifies nominal alloy compositions and measured Cu-Ni-Fe film compositions after six months in flowing seawater; those film values should not be treated as bulk alloy grade compositions.

From text 'banning1973corrosionresistanceof pages 16-19'.

LH Banning and LL Oden. Corrosion resistance of metals in hot brines: a literature review. Unknown journal, 1973.

The excerpt provides only the Banning and Oden 1973 material, not the requested Gdowski 1991, Ravindran 1983, or Lewis and LaQue 1981 tables. In Banning and Oden, Table 7 gives alloy specifications/ranges rather than measured composition results. C122 is phosphorus-deoxidized copper with 99.9% Cu+Ag and 0.015–0.040% P. C608 aluminum bronze is listed with 99.5% Cu+Ag, approximately 0.10% Fe, 5.0–6.5% Al, 0.35% As, and 0.10% Pb; C613 is listed with 99.5% Cu+Ag, 3.5% Fe, 0.2–0.5% Sn, and 6.0–8.0% Al. C706 (10% Cu-Ni) has 99.5% Cu+Ag, 1.0–1.8% Fe, and 9–11% Ni. C715 (30% Cu-Ni) has 99.5% Cu+Ag, 0.4–0.7% Fe, and 29–33% Ni. Table 8 reports corrosion in mils per year, not mdd. At 250°F seawater and 4 ft/s after 697 days, C122 measured 0.99 mpy and C608 measured 0.75 mpy. The displayed excerpt cuts off before the 697-day, 4-ft/s values for C613, C706, and C715. Testing used a recirculating brine-heater simulation loop with controlled pH, dissolved oxygen, salinity, temperature, residence time, and velocity.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.

before.title: Before

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2

        - PHASE4: Phase 4

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed

        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting

        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing

        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies

        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.

Abstract:
The suitability of copper nickel alloys for use in components of Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) systems is examined by scrutiny of data from appropriate tests and records in related applications. Copper-nickel alloy C70600 is found to exhibit excellent corrosion resistance against seawater flow rates up to 3.0 m/s. The copper-nickels are found to be galvanically compatible as a family and with other copper-base alloys in seawater. Their corrosion rate is found not to be significantly influenced by ambient variations in oxygen content, temperature, or other parameters which change with depth. Low level chlorination does not adversely affect these alloys. Adverse effects of sulfide are not anticipated. The copper-nickel alloys have excellent resistance to macrobiological fouling in seawater, but microfouling still occurs to a limited extent. The danger of leakage of ammonia into seawater, and vice versa, is found to effectively remove copper-nickel alloys as candidates for use in OTEC heat exchangers in contact with ammonia as a working fluid. 132 references. (LEW)

Abstract:
Due to its excellent performance, 90-10 cupronickel has been widely used as a pipeline for marine engineering. However, due to the harsh service conditions of flowing seawater, the problem of corrosion leakage is extremely serious. One of the most common locations is the welding joint. In this paper, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, surface morphology analysis techniques (scanning electron spectroscopy, energy disperse spectroscopy, three-dimensional microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy) are used to study the corrosion resistance of 90-10 cupronickel (MZ), heat affected zone (HAZ) and welding zone (WZ). The experimental results show that MZ, HAZ and WZ can form protective corrosion product film in flowing seawater, and that the corrosion resistance increases with the experiment time increasing and achieves the maximum value after 20 days. However, the corrosion resistance of HAZ is smallest due to the low adhesion density of corrosion production formed on HAZ. HAZ is preferentially corroded for minimum corrosion resistance and galvanic corrosion between WZ and HAZ.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Seawater emerges as a promising source of renewable energy that generates electricity by utilizing the conductive properties of saline water. A seawater-lamp-based energy device can produce low-voltage power through electrochemical reactions between dissimilar metal electrodes. Nonetheless, the presence of a complex ionic composition of seawater creates a harsh corrosive environment, hence reducing the electrode’s longevity. Despite increasing interest in seawater batteries, a research gap remains regarding the comparison of the role of chloride concentration on corrosion behaviour in natural seawater versus simplified salt solutions in active electrical circuits. Copper (Cu) and aluminium (Al) electrode pairs, which offer high potential difference and low material costs, were selected to address the lack of studies on accelerated corrosion data for seawater batteries. The aim of this study is to investigate the effects of varying chloride concentrations on electrode corrosion by comparing natural seawater with prepared sodium chloride (NaCl) solutions. Cu-Al electrode pairs were connected to a 2.5 V light bulb and utilized an impressed current. Corrosion rates were determined using the weight-loss method, while the surface characterization of electrode deposition was further determined by optical microscopy, Scanning Electron Microscopy/Energy Dispersive X-ray (SEM/EDX), and Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR). The findings suggest that although seawater yielded higher electrical performance and brightest illumination, it also exhibited rapid deterioration, with Cu and Al exceeding corrosion rates of 40 mm/yr and 8 mm/yr, respectively. Overall, the study suggests that seawater is a viable energy source for the development of low-cost, off-grid lighting due to its abundant availability and low environmental impact.</jats:p>

2.2   Less Important Forms o f Corrosion


           I n the RRGE systems the  f o l l o w i n g forms o f corrosion are thought  t o
be   l e s s important than those discussed   i n Section  2.1.


      2.2.1      Galvanic Corrosion


     Galvanic corrosion   i s the accelerated wastage o f metal due  t o the
galvanic a c t i o n o f two d i s s i m i l a r metals   i n contact.   While both m e t a l l i c
members o f  t h e s t r u c t u r e may be corroded,  the   l e s s  r e s i s t a n t member
shows an increase   i n corrosion  r a t e w h i l e the more  r e s i s t a n t corrodes
 l e s s than  i f  i t alone were exposed  t o the environment,   The more  r e s i s t a n t
member   i s s a i d  t o be cathodic and the   l e s s  r e s i s t a n t member anodic.  The
parameters  t h a t are important   i n galvanic corrosion are the  r e l a t i v e
electrochemical a c t i v i t i e s o f the two metals,  the temperature,  the
r e l a t i v e areas o f the two metals,  and the chemistry o f the environment.


     The p o t e n t i a l differences between various metals   i n geothermal
b r i n e s has n o t been studied.   However,  the  r e l a t i v e ranking o f a numberof alloys   i n sea water (Figure 2.2.1)  has been made and can serve as a
guide in predicting the behavior of these materials  in geothermal  brines
that have been cooled to about 15C (288K) to 25C (29810.  Some galvanic
potentials have been measured.   For example, Brown ('1   studied the
potentials of a number of aluminum alloys  vs.  annealed copper, hard
drawn copper and brass.   While Brown's study was conducted  a t about 2OC
(29310   i n tap and   i n distilled water,  his results indicate  t h a t large
electrochemical potentials can occur between the materials  he studied.


     Temperature effects   i n galvanic corrosion are not unusual;   thus,
as the temperature increases the rate of corrosion also increases.
However, the rate of change of electrochemical  potential  with temp-
erature  i s not the same for a l l metals.   For example,  a t room temp-
erature zinc    i s anodic with respect  t o iron.   As the temperature in-
creases   t h e potentials converge and a t some elevated temperature   t h e
iron may become anodic with respect  t o zinc (11).


     Galvanic corrosion may be combined w i t h other forms of corrosion.
For example,  if the solution    i s in the nearly neutral   t o moderately
basic pH range a coating of Fe(OH)3 forms on the iron and pitting
crevice corrosion can occur.


     Aluminum heat exchanger tubes have been considered for the primary
heat transfer system of the RRGE demonstration plant.   The possibility
t h a t a reaction can take place between the heat exchanger tubes and
copper  t h a t may occur naturally   i n the Raft River geothermal  brine
places a serious limitation on the use of aluminum.  The reaction  is:

           2 A1 + 3 Cu++ = 2 A1+++  + 3 Cu

t o give a deposit of metallic copper on the aluminum tubes.   These
metallic copper deposits would act as galvanic couples and severe
pitting of the aluminum would result.   The effect of temperature  (i.e.,
the chemical kinetics) on the copper-aluminum reaction has been investigated




                                44                ..         1 - _.   I._.
by MacKinnon and Ingraham (30331)in Canada and by Malhotra (32) in the
U.S.   Their work shows that the reaction is controlled by diffusion of
copper ion through a boundary layer at the temperatures of interest in
the RRGE systems.  The effect of bicarbonate ion (present in Raft River
geothermal brines) on this reaction has been reported by Becerra and
Darb~(~~).

     Even when dissimilar metals are in contact, galvanic corrosion may
not occur or may be sufficiently slow that serious trouble or short life
is not a problem.  This can happen because one or both of the metals may
be passivated after a short time.

     The concentration of dissolved solids and the conductivity of the
Raft River geothermal brines are such that they provide a very good
electrolyte for galvanic corrosion.  The possibility of forming dissimilar
metal couples is probably highest in the cooling tower and care must be
exercised to prevent accidental coupling.  Both the hot and cold brine
transmission lines are additional sites for galvanic corrosion and
particular attention must be given to materials selection and procurement
to insure that galvanic corrosion is prevented or controlled.

     Hermannsson (16)  noted that zinc on galvanized iron was severely
attacked in Icelandic geothermal waters containing more than about 1 ppm
dissolved oxygen.  This attack is attributed  t o galvanic corrosion
resulting from the depolarization o f both iron and zinc surfaces.  One
must cbnclude that the propensity for galvanic attack is even greater in
the more saline Raft River geothermal brines.

These will consist of bench-scale simulations, large-scale simulations and finally in-situ testing. Dr. Anan-

   Air/steam test parameters include temperatures of 150°C, 200°C, 250°C, and 300°C (the waste package
surface will see about 225°C max. in service); steam which is air-saturated at 49°C with GR4 groundwater
and distilled water flowing at 233 l/day/7.21 of chamber volume. In the pressure vessel, temperatures range
from 50C to 200°C, pressure depends on the heating conditions, and the vessels will contain 28 g of packing
material and 66 ml of groundwater. Autoclave parameters are similar to those in the pressure vessel, except
that a flow of 6 ml/hr/1 of autoclave volume will be imposed, and the pressure will be held at 1000 psi,
Specimens in the autoclaves are imbedded in packing.

    All these tests will by conducted on both long- and short-term bases. Long-term testing will proceed for
42 months with intermediate inspections at 1,4,10,18 and 28 months. Support of license applications will
probably mean that testing will continue for 10 to 20 years.

   Some data are available. Air/steam tests of phosphorus deoxidized copper show that corrosion rates in­
crease with temperature from 150°C to 300*C after both one and four months' exposure. Rates range from
2.15 mm/yr at 150°C for one month to 41.93 mm/yr at 300°C for four months. In most cases the corrosion
rate drops between one and four months. Similar results were observed with OF copper, rates ranging from
2.45 to 57.57 mm/yr for the range of conditions given above. Corrosion rates for 90-10 copper-nickel were
significantly lower, however, as shown in Table 2.

   Cuprite (Cu20) is the major corrosion product on pure copper and minor amounts of tenorite (CuO) are
also found. In 90-10 copper-nickel exactly the opposite is observed.
