    Discussing the presence of the sulfide mineral, Dr. Anantatmula showed the Eh-Ph diagram for the sys­
tem Cu-H20-S-C02. The presence of Q12S apparently matches expected repository conditions, but much
more work needs to be done on the thermodynamic analysis to confirm this.

   General corrosion tests are being conducted under gamma field irradiation to determine the threshold
radiation level below which corrosion enhancement by groundwater radiolysis is not expected, No results
are available yet, but testing has been started at 100°C and 200°C for copper and 90-10 copper-nickel at dose
rates between 10 and 10 R/hr. Dr. Anantatmula noted that the higher dose rate would be far above that
expected near actual containers in the repository.

    Pitting corrosion tests are based on potentiodynamic curve generation to establish the pitting potential.
Also, corrosion potential and polarization resistance monitoring will establish the free corrosion potentials
and detect the onsat of pitting, if any, under repository conditions. Finally, controlled potential pit growth
measurements will establish pit growth kinetics under "forced pitting" conditions, Early results indicate that
OF copper at 200°C (1 week hold) displays what may be a pitting potential at around 0.14 V (SHE), and Ecorr
is -0.89 V (SHE), Copper-nickel 90-10 shows similar behavior, but even though pitting potentials may be
observed, Dr. Anantatmula was quick to point out that actual pitting had not been produced.

   The corrosion potential of copper drops with time (up to 2000 hr) at both 150°C and 200°C. At no time
does it approach the pitting potential, which remains comfortably higher at both temperatures. The cor­
rosion potential of 90-10 Cu-Ni similarly decreases (to more negative values) with time. At 150°C it begins
at about -0.400 V, dropping to about -0350 V after 2000 hrs. At 200"C the corrosion potential remains be­
tween -0.500 and -0.600 V. The pitting potential at 200°C is -0.160 V. Dr. Anantatmula concluded that pit­
ting of a copper or a copper-nickel container is unlikely in a nuclear waste repository in basalt.

   Environmentally assisted cracking (EAC) must be evaluated to insure that it will not compromise the in­
tegrity of the container. Slow strain rate tests have shown that no EAC occurs in OF copper or 90-10 cop­
per-nickel, that minor EAC occurs in A-27 cast steels, and that pronounced EAC can be identified in A-387
low alloy steel. These results merely provide a ranking of susceptibility and are not to be construed as a go-
no-go test for the acceptance or rejection of materials. Fracture mechanics testing of the copper metals has
not yet begun; it is continuing on the steels.

WHC. These experiments are currently being performed with spent fuel + copper + groundwater and

1000 hrs.) show no significant differences  in the behavior of copper and carbon steel on radionuclide

Abstract:
Copper-based materials have long been used for their outstanding thermal and electrical conductivities in various applications, such as heat exchangers, induction heat coils, cooling channels, radiators, and electronic connectors. The development of advanced copper alloys has broadened their utilization to include structural applications in harsh service conditions found in industries like oil and gas, marine, power plants, and water treatment, where good corrosion resistance and a combination of high strength, wear, and fatigue tolerance are critical. These advanced multi-component structures often have complex designs and intricate geometries, requiring extensive metallurgical processing routes and the joining of the individual components into a final structure. Additive manufacturing (AM) has revolutionized the way complex structures are designed and manufactured. It has reduced the processing steps, assemblies, and tooling while also eliminating the need for joining processes. However, the high thermal conductivity of copper and its high reflectivity to near-infrared radiation present challenges in the production of copper alloys using fusion-based AM processes, especially with Yb-fiber laser-based techniques. To overcome these difficulties, various solutions have been proposed, such as the use of high-power, low-wavelength laser sources, preheating the build chamber, employing low thermal conductivity building platforms, and adding alloying elements or composite particles to the feedstock material. This article systematically reviews different aspects of AM processing of common industrial copper alloys and composites, including copper-chrome, copper-nickel, tin-bronze, nickel-aluminum bronze, copper-carbon composites, copper-ceramic composites, and copper-metal composites. It focuses on the state-of-the-art AM techniques employed for processing different copper-based materials and the associated technological and metallurgical challenges, optimized processing variables, the impact of post-printing heat treatments, the resulting microstructural features, physical properties, mechanical performance, and corrosion response of the AM-fabricated parts. Where applicable, a comprehensive comparison of the results with those of their conventionally fabricated counterparts is provided.

     Aluminum alloys 1100, 3003, 5005, 5052, 5454, 5554, 6061, 6063, and 6061
 clad were among families of alloys investigated by the Dow Chemical Co. at
Freeport, Tex. (31, p. 464). It was stated that the optimum initial immer-
sion conditions for aluminum appears to be 50 to 100 ppb dissolved oxygen in
sea water having a pH from 5.0 to 5.5. After a conditioning period of 10 to
24 hours, aluminum corrosion rates become independent of dissolved oxygen.
For continued absence of pitting, a pH of 6 was considered optimum. The
effect of velocity on pitting attack varied with the alloy being investigated.
Alloy 5005 showed increased pitting with increased velocity, some of the
others showed less. Increas ing temperature from 1800 to 2250 F approximately
doubled the corrosion rate while the frequency of pitting decreased. Test
results indicated that alloys 3003 and 5454 were the preferred ones for

     Water chemistry is one of the factors affecting materials performance in
desalination environments being investigated by OSW. The fifth progress
report on behavior of metals in desalination environments published by the
National Association of Corrosion Engine2rs (NACE) (36) describes recent
investigations on aluminum alloys. Some information is given on steel (1010)
and copper-base alloys. Conclusions of this report are particularly note-
worthy and follow:

     Resul ts of electrochemical, weight loss, and visual pitting observa-
     tions show that a sea water pH of 6.0 is optimum for aluminum
     alloys in normal sea water over a temperature range of 180-2500 F.

     Of the aluminum alloys tested. under the above conditions, alloys
     3003, 5052, and 5454 performed the best.

     Studies of aluminum alloys over a l2-month period in 180-2500 F
     sea water show the alloys to be independent of dissolved oxygen
      in the range of ~5 to 1,000 ppb. This information should be of
     practical value for the use of aluminum in desalting practice.

     Bicarbonate alkalinity values approximating 20 ppm appear to be
     beneficial to the performance of aluminum alloys in hot sea
     water.                                                                                        11


     Alloys of aluminum copper, and steel experienced higher corrosion
     rates when subj ected to chlorinated sea water during the early
     portion of exposure. Surface inspections show that chlorination
     may disrupt the protective film of aluminum and copper alloys
     in particular.

     The work on chlorination suggests that the solid state products
     resulting from the reaction between chlorine and the various
     organic and metal ion consti tuents of the sea water are not
     removed by deaeration and function as corrodants when in contact
    with certain metal surfaces.

     During 1970, research was initiated by OSW (31, p. 451) to develop
fundamental knowledge concerning the behavior of aluminum in desalination
equipment. These studies were started because of the unexpected galvanic
attack between aluminum alloys in the brine heater of the OSW pilot plant
(built by Reynolds Metals Co.) at Wrightsville Beach, N.C., because of the
excessively rapid dissipation of the cladding on Alclad tubes, and because
of the rapid utilization of aluminum anodes in the hot and evaporator sections.

     Investigators of the Reynolds Metals Co. (35) reported on the electro-
chemical performance of aluminum alloys under distillation desalination plant
water chemistry conditions. Potentiometric testing of several aluminum alloys
revealed that there is considerable instability of potential during the first
few hours of exposure of most aluminum alloys to saline solutions; such
instability of potential could be instrumental to initiating corrosive attack.
Their investigation indicated that alloys containing 0.9 percent or more
magnesium may be subject to serious pitting corrosion problems. Some alloys
have a dual temperature-potential curve. Of the 5,000 series alloys, which
are prime candidates for desalination service, only alloy 5005 had a single
temperature-potential curve.

     Other studies of the Reynolds investigators included alloy composition
solution velocity, weldment performance, cold work on potential, and low-
oxygen content of solutions. Comments on only a few of tHese are included
here:

     At 3000 F and above, copper content had no effect on potentials;
     at lower temperatures there were both positive and negative effects.

     Nei ther iron nor silicon, in quanti ties usually found in aluminum
     alloys, had a significant effect on potentials.

     Zinc caused a negative shift in potential that became less evident
     with increasing temperature.

     They found that alloys of relatively high purity would be desirable
for plant construction because of the effects of alloying constituents and
temperature on corrosion potential; alloys 1235 and 5005 were favored.
They were of the opinion that steady high-temperature operations would not
be a serious problem for aluminum alloys.12


     Laboratory work in which the electrochemical potential behavior of
various aluminum alloys in pilot plant environments of a distillation desalt-
ing process was described by Snodgrass (37). Polarization and transient
voltage measurements were also made. Transient voltage measurements can be
used to detect active pitting on aluminum alloys. Although not fully
developed, such measurements appear to have great utility in studying effects
of parameters such as pH and chloride concentration on corrosion.

apparent. Aluminum has been found satisfactory at The Geysers for circulating
water lines (~), aluminum butterfly valves in aluminum pipe risers of cooling
towers, tubes in turbine oil coolers, and as exterior sheathing on buildings.
When exposed to condensate for 150 days at the geothermal field in Hveragerdi,
Iceland, pure aluminum was one of the few materials that showed no visible
corrosion (13).

geothermal fluids of the Cerro Prieto field. Aluminum (99.9+ percent Al) was
used in tests in separated aerated steam, separated condensed steam at low
velocity, separated condensed steam at high velocity, and in atmospheric
exposure tests (38). The only material of those tested that exhibited corro-
sion resistance superior to aluminum in separated aerated steam was
Stellite 6, a high-cobalt alloy; the only material that exhibited signifi-
cantly superior corrosion resistance in separated condensed steam of low
velocity was an austenitic stainless steel, AISI 304; and the only materials
that exhibited superior corrosion resistance in separated condensed steam of
high velocity were stainless steels AISI 304 and AISI 410. In the atmospheric
exposure tes ts, no material was significantly superior to aluminum.

     Copper and copper-base alloys have a unique combination of properties
that make them an excellent choice for many hot concentrated brine applica-
tions. In addition to their excellent heat conductivity, some alloys are
practically immune to stress corrosion cracking while having good resistance
to general corrosion. Furthermore, copper is the most resistant metal to

                                   In Sea Water

     The most important factor affecting the corrosion of copper and its
alloys in sea water is oxyten. Fi~k (ll, p. 7) states that oxygen causes
depolarization of cathodic areas, it may oxidize metal ions in solution to
a higher valence state, and it may promote formation of a protective film on                                                                                  13


the metal surface. Experiments at 3000 to 3100 F have shown that copper ion
pickup in sea water has been decreased from 23 parts per million before
deaeration to only 0.17 part per million after deaeration.

     Materials Selector (28) gives the following pertinent corrosion
information:

     For copper: 0.5 to 2 mils per year (mpy) typical in shallow and
     deep ocean; lower rates reported, e.g., 0.38 mpy after 16 years
     in shallow depths of Pacific off Panama Canal. Single phase
     brasses, silicon and phosphor bronzes are generally similar.
     Beryllium-copper slightly more resistant. Resistance of iron-
     modified 194 seems to be considerably greater than for copper.
     Brasses vary in resistance; high zinc grades tend to fail by
     dezincification, especially those of two or more phases. Alloys
     with 15% Zn or less not as apt to fail in this manner. Red brass,
     alloy 230, similar to copper (0.5 to 2 mpy) in deep and shallow
     waters. Arsenic inhibited admiralty brass also resistant (0.6 mpy
     after 3 years in both deep and shallow waters). Aluminum brass
     (Alloy 687) has very high resistance; 0.7 mpy after 5 months,
     0.2 mpy after 3 years at 6,000 feet. Silicon bronze similar to
     copper in rate of attack. 5% aluminum bronze has high resistance
     (?l mpy after several months, 0.3 mpy after 3 years). 7% aluminum
     bronze prone to dealuminumization. Cupronickels have high resist-
     ance; 0.1 to 1.3 mpy after several months, about 0.8 mpy after
      3 years.

## 1. Effect of Al Element on the Microstructure and Properties of Cu-Ni-Fe-Mn Alloys
Valid Text Names:
'yang2018effectofal pages 1-3', 'yang2018effectofal pages 3-7', 'yang2018effectofal pages 7-9', 'yang2018effectofal pages 9-11'

BibTex:
@article{yang2018effectofal,
    author = "Yang, Ran and Wen, Jiuba and Zhou, Yanjun and Song, Kexing and Song, Zhengcheng",
    title = "Effect of Al Element on the Microstructure and Properties of Cu-Ni-Fe-Mn Alloys",
    year = "2018",
    journal = "Materials",
    volume = "11",
    pages = "1777",
    month = "Sep",
    doi = "10.3390/ma11091777",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/ma11091777",
    publisher = "MDPI AG",
    issue = "9",
    issn = "1996-1944"
}


Abstract:
The effects of aluminum on the mechanical properties and corrosion behavior in artificial seawater of Cu-Ni-Fe-Mn alloys were investigated. Cu-7Ni-xAl-1Fe-1Mn samples, consisting of 0, 1, 3, 5, and 7 wt % aluminum along with the same contents of other alloying elements (Ni, Fe, and Mn), were prepared. The microstructure of Cu-7Ni-xAl-1Fe-1Mn alloy was analyzed by Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), and its corrosion property was tested by an electrochemical system. The results show that the mechanical and corrosion properties of Cu-7Ni-xAl-1Fe-1Mn alloy have an obvious change with the aluminum content. The tensile strength has a peak value of 395 MPa by adding 3 wt % aluminum in the alloy. Moreover, the corrosion rate in artificial seawater of Cu-7Ni-3Al-1Fe-1Mn alloy is 0.0215 mm/a which exhibits a better corrosion resistance than the commercially used UNS C70600. It is confirmed that the second-phase transformation of Cu-7Ni-xAl-1Fe-1Mn alloy follows the sequence of α solid solution → Ni3Al → Ni3Al + NiAl → Ni3Al + NiAl3. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) shows that the adding element aluminum in the Cupronickel can improve the corrosion resistance of Cu-7Ni-xAl-1Fe-1Mn alloy.

Abstract:
The 70/30 copper–nickel alloy is used mainly in critical parts with more demanding conditions in marine settings. There is a need for innovative methods that offer fast production and cost-effectiveness in order to supplement current copper–nickel alloy manufacturing processes. In this study, we employ wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) to fabricate the 70/30 copper–nickel alloy. The as-built microstructure is characterized by columnar grains with prominent dendrites and chemical segregation in the inter-dendritic area. The aspect ratio of the columnar grain increases with increasing travel speed (TS) at the same wire feed speed (WFS). This is in contrast with the equiaxed grain structure, with a more random orientation, of the conventional sample. The sample built with a WFS of 8 m/min, TS of 1000 mm/min, and a track distance of 3.85 mm exhibits superior corrosion properties in the 3.5 wt% NaCl solution when compared with the conventional sample, as evidenced by a higher film resistance and breakdown potential, along with a lower passive current density of the WAAM sample. The corrosion morphology reveals the critical roles played by the nickel element that is unevenly distributed between the dendrite core and inter-dendritic area.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Monel-400, a nickel-copper-based alloy, is renowned for its exceptional corrosion resistance, high strength, and toughness across diverse operating environments. However, these desirable properties also make Monel-400 a challenging material to machine using conventional techniques, leading to excessive tool wear, poor surface finish, and high thermal stresses. There is currently no comprehensive review that systematically consolidates and compares non-conventional machining approaches applied to Monel-400 alloy. This review critically examines the non-conventional machining methods employed to address these challenges, including Electric Discharge Machining (EDM), Wire EDM (WEDM), Electrochemical Machining (ECM), Plasma Arc Cutting (PAC), Abrasive Water Jet Machining (AWJM), Photochemical Machining (PCM), and Hot Machining. A systematic comparison of process performance, surface integrity, material removal rate (MRR), Tool Wear Rate (TWR), Surface Roughness (Ra), and optimization strategies is presented. Key advancements such as hybrid dielectrics, cryogenic treatments, near-dry machining, and AI-based optimization techniques are discussed. Challenges related to surface defects, environmental sustainability, tool degradation, and process scalability are highlighted, along with identified research gaps. Future research directions emphasize the development of eco-friendly machining solutions, hybrid machining systems, real-time adaptive control, and life cycle assessments to enable sustainable industrial applications. This review consolidates fragmented knowledge, provides a roadmap for future innovation, and supports the advancement of efficient, precise, and environmentally responsible machining practices for Monel-400.</jats:p>

This excerpt describes Alfantazi, Ahmed, and Tromans (2009), which examined copper-alloy electrochemical behavior using potentiodynamic polarization rather than reporting a same-test mass-loss corrosion-rate series. Tests used 1 M NaCl at pH 6.5 and 10, including buffered and unbuffered chloride conditions. The alloys were commercial solid-solution materials with nominal compositions Cu–30Ni, Cu–30Zn, and 90Cu–8Al–2Fe (aluminum bronze); pure copper was also tested as a reference. At pH 6.5, the polarization response showed no evidence of passivity and was dominated by copper. At pH 10, limited passivity appeared, especially in buffered chloride, with Cu–Zn showing pronounced passivity over a broad potential range. Increasing anodic potential beyond a critical film-breakdown potential caused a sharp current increase. The excerpt mentions prior seawater work on 90Cu–10Ni and 70Cu–30Ni, including oxygen-concentration effects, but does not provide the numerical rates, test duration, detailed method, or exact tables/figures for those studies. Effect of seawater level on corrosion behavior of different alloys

                     Saleh A. Al-Fozan, Anees U. Malik*

                      PO Box 8328, Al-Jubail 31951, Saudi Arabia

                            Received 7 February 2006; Accepted 12 August 2007





Abstract

   Seawater is inherently chemically aggressive, and therefore, constructional materials used in seawater handling
and processing systems including desalination plants are subjected to varying degree of corrosion depending upon
the nature of the material(s) and operational conditions. Broadly speaking, for applications in seawater, the materials
are usually exposed to three zones, namely, fully immersed, partially immersed or seawater surrounding environment.
Interestingly, from corrosion point of view, the seawater behaves differently under the aforementioned conditions.
A study was undertaken to investigate the effect of seawater level on a number of alloys having wide applications
as structural materials in seawater processing plants. The laboratory immersion test technique has been applied to
evaluate the effect of seawater level on the corrosion behavior of different alloys. In three sets of experiments, carbon
steels (G1010 and 1020), austenitic stainless steels (304 SS and 316L SS), cupro-nickel (90/10 Cu/Ni and 70/30
Cu/Ni), Ni-based alloys (Incoloy 825 and Inconel 625) were utilized. The specimens were fixed at three locations
namely, above seawater surface, semi submerged in seawater and fully submerged in seawater. The experiments were
carried out at room temperature with very slow seawater movement (12 L/h). The exposure time was varied between
1–2 years. In this study the corrosion behavior of different alloys has been evaluated based on exposure location.
Besides corrosion rate calculations, the localized attack has also been discussed on the basis of the magnitude of pit
depths.

R. O. Lewis and F. Laque. Evaluation of copper-nickel alloys for otec applications. ArXiv, Apr 1981. URL: https://doi.org/10.2172/6255887, doi:10.2172/6255887. This article has 5 citations.

The Lewis and LaQue (1981) excerpt provides Table XIV data for uncoupled alloys after one-year exposures in 0.6 m/s flowing seawater, using equal-area galvanic couples. The uncoupled corrosion rate for C70600 copper-nickel alloy was 30.5 µm/y (1.2 mpy), while C71500 was 20.3 µm/y (0.8 mpy). Aluminum bronze had an uncoupled rate of 43.2 µm/y (1.7 mpy), and nickel-aluminum bronze measured 150.0 µm/y (5.9 mpy). Carbon steel and titanium are also listed at 330.0 µm/y (13.0 mpy) and less than 2.5 µm/y (less than 0.1 mpy), respectively. These are measured corrosion-rate results, not alloy composition specifications: the excerpt identifies alloys by UNS designations and does not provide their exact measured weight-percent compositions. The excerpt does not contain the requested Gdowski Table 34/35, Ravindran Table 5, or Banning Oden Tables 7/8 data, so it cannot support exact ocean depth, exposure duration, alloy-form, weighing-method, or composition details from those sources.

{"answer": "## Same-test seawater comparisons

The clearest natural-seawater comparison is a 120-day field test of copper, 90–10 Cu–Ni and 70–30 Cu–Ni. A second field dataset compares copper with Cu–30Ni over several longer exposures. The tables below preserve the sources’ reported rates and units; an alloy designation or specification range is **not** a measured specimen composition. (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000009)

**Ravindran, K. (1983), “Copper-Nickel Alloys for Marine Aquacultural Engineering,” *Fishery Technology* 20, Table 5; DOI not identified.** Metal panels were exposed together for **120 days** in natural seawater at Cochin Harbour, with tidal flushing and water velocity ranging from still to **0.80 m s⁻¹**. The source does not give a test-water temperature or explicitly state how the corrosion rates were measured; these must **not** be called confirmed weight-loss rates. Copper is identified as CDA 110, and the Cu–Ni plates were supplied by International Nickel; measured specimen assays are not given. The 90–10 and 70–30 descriptions imply *nominal*, not analytically verified, **10 and 30 wt% Ni**, respectively. (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000050)

| Table 5 material | Product form | Corrosion rate, exactly as tabulated |
|---|---|---:|
| Copper, CDA 110; Ni content not reported | Plate/panel | **61.0 micron year⁻¹** |
| 90–10 copper-nickel; nominal 10 wt% Ni | Plate/panel | **22.5 micron year⁻¹** |
| 70–30 copper-nickel; nominal 30 wt% Ni | Plate/panel | **22.5 micron year⁻¹** |

The rates and their shared exposure appear together in **Table 5**, not in the article’s separate biofouling table. (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000042)

**Wheatfall (1967), as reproduced in G. E. Gdowski (1991), *Survey of Degradation Modes of Four Nickel-Chromium-Molybdenum Alloys*, DOI: [10.2172/138275](https://doi.org/10.2172/138275).** Gdowski is a **compilation**, not the original experiment; an original Wheatfall DOI was not identified. Its **Table 34** reports mass-loss rates in **mdd (mg dm⁻² day⁻¹)** for unalloyed copper and “Cu-Ni(30)” (nominal 30 wt% Ni); **Table 35** supplies their shared natural-seawater exposure conditions. Specimen product form and measured wt% assays are not stated. Deep-water exposures had currents **<0.5 knot**; the surface exposure had **1–2 knots**. (pqac-00000009)

| Exposure: depth; duration; temperature — Table 35 | Unalloyed Cu — Table 34 | Cu–Ni(30) — Table 34 |
|---|---:|---:|
| **5,640 ft; 123 days; 2.78°C** | **12.1 mdd** | **6.27 mdd** |
| **5,640 ft; 751 days; 2.39°C** | **3.78 mdd** | **2.75 mdd** |
| **5,300 ft; 1,064 days; 2.50°C** | **2.65 mdd** | **3.08 mdd** |
| **Surface; 386 days; 17.61°C** | **4.50 mdd** | **1.42 mdd** |

These results do **not** establish that Cu–30Ni always has the lower rate: copper is lower in the **1,064-day** exposure. Table 34 flags the **4.50 mdd** copper result as weight loss attributed largely to localized corrosion, so it should not be interpreted as a uniform penetration rate. (pqac-00000009)

## Same-test copper, Cu–Ni and specified aluminum bronzes

**Cohen, A., and A. L. Whitted (1971), “Copper and Its Alloys in the Desalting Environment,” *Corrosion/71*, Paper 57; original DOI not identified.** The numerical results and nominal alloy specifications are reproduced in **L. H. Banning and L. L. Oden (1973), *Corrosion Resistance of Metals in Hot Brines: A Literature Review*, U.S. Bureau of Mines Information Circular 8601, Tables 7–8**. Banning and Oden is a **government literature compilation**; no DOI was identified for it. This is a particularly useful *same-loop* copper/bronze/Cu–Ni comparison, but it represents **treated, hot, flowing seawater**, not quiet ambient immersion. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000051)

The brine-heater simulation used seawater at **250°F**, pH **7.4**, **83%** of normal seawater salinity, **3 ppm CO₂**, and **72 ppb dissolved oxygen in make-up water**. Table 8 separately reports **4, 8 and 16 ft s⁻¹** and **90, 170 and 697 days**. The directly matched **4-ft-s⁻¹, 697-day** column is transcribed below. The retrieved account does not establish the specimens’ product form or explicitly identify the rate calculation as weight loss. **Table 7 contains nominal composition limits, not measured analyses**, and its “Cu+Ag” entries cannot be read as 99.5 wt% copper *in addition to* the listed Ni or Al. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025)

| Material; Table 7 nominal composition, wt% | Table 8 corrosion rate: 4 ft s⁻¹, 697 days |
|---|---:|
| **C122**, phosphorus-deoxidized copper: Cu+Ag **≥99.9**, P **0.015–0.040** | **0.99 mpy** |
| **C608**, aluminum bronze: Al **5.0–6.5**, Fe **≤0.10** | **0.75 mpy** |
| **C613**, aluminum bronze: Al **6.0–8.0**, Fe **≤3.5**, Sn **0.2–0.5** | **0.73 mpy** |
| **C706**, 90–10 Cu–Ni: Ni **9–11**, Fe **1.0–1.8** | **0.70 mpy** |
| **C715**, 70–30 Cu–Ni: Ni **29–33**, Fe **0.4–0.7** | **0.46 mpy** |

All five numbers are from the **same Table 8 column**, rather than rates assembled from different tests. Table 7 is the source of the stated wt% *specifications*. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026)

A further bronze comparison is **R. O. Lewis and F. LaQue (1981), *Evaluation of Copper-Nickel Alloys for OTEC Applications*, DOI: [10.2172/6255887](https://doi.org/10.2172/6255887), Table XIV**. This is a **DOE compilation of “Inco Unpublished Data.”** Its *uncoupled* specimens were exposed for **one year** in seawater flowing at **0.6 m s⁻¹**: aluminum bronze, **43.2 µm/y (1.7 mpy)**; C70600, **30.5 µm/y (1.2 mpy)**; C71500, **20.3 µm/y (0.8 mpy)**. Table XIV does **not** identify the aluminum-bronze grade or establish that it contains 5–9 wt% Al; nor does it give specimen form, temperature, measured compositions or an explicit mass-loss method. It is therefore a useful bronze/Cu–Ni comparison, but **not a verified Cu–5Al-to-Cu–9Al comparison**. These are the *uncoupled* rows, not the table’s galvanically coupled results. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000043)

## Scope and remaining gap

An additional **peer-reviewed, weight-loss** Cu–Ni comparison—but **without copper or bronze**—is **S. A. Al-Fozan and A. U. Malik (2008), *Desalination* 228:61–67, DOI: [10.1016/j.desal.2007.08.007](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.desal.2007.08.007)**. Rectangular **50 × 20 × 2 mm** specimens were fully immersed in slowly moving (**12 L h⁻¹**) Arabian Gulf seawater at **25 ± 5°C**. **Table 1** gives measured compositions, wt%: 90/10 Cu–Ni **Cu 88.18, Ni 9.93, Fe 1.41, Mn 0.273**; 70/30 Cu–Ni **Cu 68.81, Ni 30, Fe 0.53, Mn 0.51**. In **Table 3**, fully submerged 90/10 specimens measured **0.145 mpy at 198 days** and **0.082 mpy at 401 days**; 70/30 specimens measured **0.067 mpy at 192 days** and **0.049 mpy at 365 days**. The exposure durations differ by alloy, so even these are **same-study, same-conditions results, not exact same-duration pairs**. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040)

**No verified same-test numerical series containing intermediate Cu–2Ni or Cu–5Ni alongside Cu–10Ni and Cu–30Ni was located.** Ravindran and the Cohen–Whitted compilation supply the narrower **Cu/10Ni/30Ni** progression, with the composition and method qualifications above. Neither a Cu–Ni-only quiet-water table nor a polarization curve has been substituted for the requested copper-versus-Cu–Ni mass-loss evidence. (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025)"}

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide the requested Campbell, Radford, Tuck, and Barker (2002) CORROSION 58:57–71 table of all-same-test isolated weight-loss rates for pure copper, C70600 (90/10 copper-nickel), C71500 (70/30 copper-nickel), aluminum bronze, and MARINEL. It also lacks the requested exact alloy compositions, specimen forms, test temperature, flow rate, and exposure durations for that comparison. However, it supplies several related seawater and desalination comparisons. In tropical marine exposure, 70/30 copper-nickel and aluminum bronze showed excellent corrosion resistance; after 16 years, reported average penetrations were 2.25 mils for 70/30 copper-nickel and 1.26 mils for aluminum bronze. A seawater-materials review states that 90/10 copper-nickel is generally superior to aluminum brass, especially at elevated temperatures and high velocities, and recommends matching or cladding tubesheets with tube material. Key West quiescent-seawater tests found C70600 and C71500 virtually immune to de-alloying, with intermediate fouling. A Delaware River brackish-water study reported that 70/30 copper-nickel experienced plug de-nickelification and 3–5 mils/year general corrosion at low velocities. Desalination tests reported low metal losses and no pitting or preferential weld attack, but used controlled pH rather than natural seawater. These sources provide qualitative and selected comparative corrosion evidence, not the exact requested same-test dataset.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes Alfantazi, Ahmed, and Tromans (2009), which examined copper-alloy electrochemical behavior using potentiodynamic polarization rather than reporting a same-test mass-loss corrosion-rate series. Tests used 1 M NaCl at pH 6.5 and 10, including buffered and unbuffered chloride conditions. The alloys were commercial solid-solution materials with nominal compositions Cu–30Ni, Cu–30Zn, and 90Cu–8Al–2Fe (aluminum bronze); pure copper was also tested as a reference. At pH 6.5, the polarization response showed no evidence of passivity and was dominated by copper. At pH 10, limited passivity appeared, especially in buffered chloride, with Cu–Zn showing pronounced passivity over a broad potential range. Increasing anodic potential beyond a critical film-breakdown potential caused a sharp current increase. The excerpt mentions prior seawater work on 90Cu–10Ni and 70Cu–30Ni, including oxygen-concentration effects, but does not provide the numerical rates, test duration, detailed method, or exact tables/figures for those studies. It therefore supplies composition and electrochemical-test context, but not the requested comparative mass-loss data for Cu, 90/10, 70/30, or aluminum bronze.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a directly relevant copper-alloy seawater test series, although it does not identify the Al-Fozan and Malik (2008), Alfantazi et al. (2009), or Ravindran (1983) studies requested. A Copper Development Association/OSW Freeport loop evaluated 12 alloys for up to 697 days under simulated desalination brine-heater conditions: 250°F seawater, pH 7.4, approximately 83% normal seawater salinity, carbon dioxide at 3 ppm, dissolved oxygen in make-up water at 72 ppb, and flow velocities of 4, 8, and 16 ft/s. The method involved treated, deaerated seawater adjusted with sodium hydroxide and controlled oxygen additions. Table 7 lists nominal compositions, including commercially pure copper (122, 142), copper-iron alloy 194, aluminum bronzes 608 (5–6.5% Al) and 613 (6–8% Al), 10% Cu-Ni 706 (9–11% Ni), 30% Cu-Ni 715 (29–33% Ni), modified 715, Cu-Ni-30% plus 5% Fe (716), and 40% Cu-Ni 720 (40–43% Ni). Table 8 reports corrosion rates in mils per year at 90, 170, and 697 days for each velocity. For example, copper 122 ranges from 0.95 to 4.20 mpy, while arsenical admiralty brass 443 ranges from 0.61 to 3.67 mpy. The excerpt begins the table but does not include all aluminum-bronze and Cu-Ni results.

Corrosion was evaluated using a static immersion mass-loss test according to JB/T 7901-1999, using cylindrical specimens measuring Φ30 mm × 2.5 mm, three parallel specimens per group, artificial seawater, room temperature, and a 10-day exposure; the seawater was replaced every seventh day. The corrosion rate was calculated from mass loss using specimen surface area, exposure time, and density. The reported rate for Cu-7Ni-3Al-1Fe-1Mn was 0.0215 mm/a, described as better than commercially used UNS C70600. Electrochemical testing additionally used artificial seawater, a graphite auxiliary electrode, and saturated calomel reference electrode. contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative results from Alfantazi, Ahmed, and Tromans (2009) for binary copper alloys tested in 1 M NaCl. The alloys examined were Cu–Ni, Cu–Al, and Cu–Zn, but the excerpt does not state their nominal compositions, numerical corrosion rates, test durations, or exact table/figure numbers containing rate data. Under open-circuit, freely corroding conditions in unbuffered chloride solution at pH 6, surface dealloying occurred early in Cu–Al and, to a much lesser extent, Cu–Zn. Localized attack was observed in both Cu–Al and Cu–Ni; the attack on Cu–Ni was more intense, and increasing electrode potential caused the localized attack to spread across the exposed surface. EDX detected chloride together with small amounts of the principal alloying elements. The corrosion product was considered mainly CuCl, with possible Ni(OH)2 or NiO in the Cu–Ni alloy. In a treated desalination environment at 250°F and 16 ft/s, 90/10 Cu-Ni (Alloy 706) had a reported corrosion rate of 2.36 mils per year, while the maximum rate among the tested alloys was 2.60 MPY. In brackish Delaware River water, 70/30 Cu-Ni experienced plug dezincification at low velocities and general corrosion of three to five mils per year. A 16-year tropical marine exposure produced average penetration of 2.25 mils for 70/30 Cu-Ni and 1.26 mils for aluminum bronze. The excerpt also states that 90/10 Cu-Ni generally outperformed aluminum brass in seawater, especially at elevated temperature and high velocity, and that both 90/10 and 70/30 Cu-Ni were virtually immune to de-alloying in quiescent seawater. These data are not directly interchangeable because test media, velocity, temperature, exposure duration, and measurement methods differ.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides the experimental basis for comparing the Al-Fozan and Malik (2008) 90/10 and 70/30 copper–nickel tests, but it does not include the numerical corrosion-rate results requested. The study tested 90/10 Cu/Ni and 70/30 Cu/Ni alongside carbon steels, stainless steels, and nickel alloys. Specimens were exposed above the seawater surface, semi-submerged, or fully submerged, at room temperature in slowly moving Arabian Gulf seawater (12 L/h), for 1–2 years. Corrosion rates were determined by the weight-loss coupon method, while pit depths were measured microscopically. Table 1 gives nominal compositions: 90/10 Cu/Ni contained approximately 88.18% Cu and 9.93% Ni, while 70/30 Cu/Ni contained approximately 68.81% Cu and 30% Ni. No commercially pure copper or aluminum bronze appears in the listed Al-Fozan/Malik test materials, so this excerpt cannot support a same-test comparison involving those alloys. Table 3 is introduced as containing corrosion rates, but its numerical contents are absent from the supplied pages. The excerpt likewise contains no information from Alfantazi, Ahmed, and Tromans (2009), Ravindran (1983), or their exact tables, figures, media conditions, and nominal compositions.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: I need SAME-TEST seawater corrosion data that compare unalloyed copper (or a copper alloy with less than 5 wt% Ni) against 90-10 copper-nickel (C70600) and/or 70-30 copper-nickel (C71500), measured in the same study under the same conditions (natural or synthetic seawater, or 3.5 wt% NaCl; quiet immersion preferred; mass loss or weight loss preferred over Tafel; 30 days or longer preferred). Also any same-study series of Cu-Ni alloys with several Ni contents between 0 and 30 wt% (for example Cu-2Ni, Cu-5Ni, Cu-10Ni, Cu-30Ni), and any same-study comparison of an aluminum bronze (Cu-5Al to Cu-9Al, with or without Fe) against a copper-nickel. For each, give: the paper (authors, year, DOI), each alloy's composition in wt%, product form, the test (medium, temperature, flow, duration, method), and each alloy's corrosion rate exactly as reported with units. List only numbers you can see in the source; say which table or figure each comes from. Prefer peer-reviewed papers and authoritative compilations (for example LaQue, Efird, the Copper Development Association, INCO/Nickel Institute), and say which are compilations.


## Same-test seawater comparisons

The clearest natural-seawater comparison is a 120-day field test of copper, 90–10 Cu–Ni and 70–30 Cu–Ni. A second field dataset compares copper with Cu–30Ni over several longer exposures. The tables below preserve the sources’ reported rates and units; an alloy designation or specification range is **not** a measured specimen composition. (ravindran1983coppernickelalloysfor pages 5-7, gdowski1991surveyofdegradation pages 44-46)

**Ravindran, K. (1983), “Copper-Nickel Alloys for Marine Aquacultural Engineering,” *Fishery Technology* 20, Table 5; DOI not identified.** Metal panels were exposed together for **120 days** in natural seawater at Cochin Harbour, with tidal flushing and water velocity ranging from still to **0.80 m s⁻¹**. The source does not give a test-water temperature or explicitly state how the corrosion rates were measured; these must **not** be called confirmed weight-loss rates. Copper is identified as CDA 110, and the Cu–Ni plates were supplied by International Nickel; measured specimen assays are not given. The 90–10 and 70–30 descriptions imply *nominal*, not analytically verified, **10 and 30 wt% Ni**, respectively. (ravindran1983coppernickelalloysfor pages 3-5, ravindran1983coppernickelalloysfor pages 5-7, ravindran1983coppernickelalloysfor media d2968613, ravindran1983coppernickelalloysfor pages 7-7)

| Table 5 material | Product form | Corrosion rate, exactly as tabulated |
|---|---|---:|
| Copper, CDA 110; Ni content not reported | Plate/panel | **61.0 micron year⁻¹** |
| 90–10 copper-nickel; nominal 10 wt% Ni | Plate/panel | **22.5 micron year⁻¹** |
| 70–30 copper-nickel; nominal 30 wt% Ni | Plate/panel | **22.5 micron year⁻¹** |

The rates and their shared exposure appear together in **Table 5**, not in the article’s separate biofouling table. (ravindran1983coppernickelalloysfor pages 5-7, ravindran1983coppernickelalloysfor media d2968613)

**Wheatfall (1967), as reproduced in G. E. Gdowski (1991), *Survey of Degradation Modes of Four Nickel-Chromium-Molybdenum Alloys*, DOI: [10.2172/138275](https://doi.org/10.2172/138275).** Gdowski is a **compilation**, not the original experiment; an original Wheatfall DOI was not identified. Its **Table 34** reports mass-loss rates in **mdd (mg dm⁻² day⁻¹)** for unalloyed copper and “Cu-Ni(30)” (nominal 30 wt% Ni); **Table 35** supplies their shared natural-seawater exposure conditions. Specimen product form and measured wt% assays are not stated. Deep-water exposures had currents **<0.5 knot**; the surface exposure had **1–2 knots**. (gdowski1991surveyofdegradation pages 44-46)

| Exposure: depth; duration; temperature — Table 35 | Unalloyed Cu — Table 34 | Cu–Ni(30) — Table 34 |
|---|---:|---:|
| **5,640 ft; 123 days; 2.78°C** | **12.1 mdd** | **6.27 mdd** |
| **5,640 ft; 751 days; 2.39°C** | **3.78 mdd** | **2.75 mdd** |
| **5,300 ft; 1,064 days; 2.50°C** | **2.65 mdd** | **3.08 mdd** |
| **Surface; 386 days; 17.61°C** | **4.50 mdd** | **1.42 mdd** |

These results do **not** establish that Cu–30Ni always has the lower rate: copper is lower in the **1,064-day** exposure. Table 34 flags the **4.50 mdd** copper result as weight loss attributed largely to localized corrosion, so it should not be interpreted as a uniform penetration rate. (gdowski1991surveyofdegradation pages 44-46)

## Same-test copper, Cu–Ni and specified aluminum bronzes

**Cohen, A., and A. L. Whitted (1971), “Copper and Its Alloys in the Desalting Environment,” *Corrosion/71*, Paper 57; original DOI not identified.** The numerical results and nominal alloy specifications are reproduced in **L. H. Banning and L. L. Oden (1973), *Corrosion Resistance of Metals in Hot Brines: A Literature Review*, U.S. Bureau of Mines Information Circular 8601, Tables 7–8**. Banning and Oden is a **government literature compilation**; no DOI was identified for it. This is a particularly useful *same-loop* copper/bronze/Cu–Ni comparison, but it represents **treated, hot, flowing seawater**, not quiet ambient immersion. (banning1973corrosionresistanceof pages 16-19, banning1973corrosionresistanceof pages 19-21, banning1973corrosionresistanceof media 97c8a396, banning1973corrosionresistanceof pages 1-4)

The brine-heater simulation used seawater at **250°F**, pH **7.4**, **83%** of normal seawater salinity, **3 ppm CO₂**, and **72 ppb dissolved oxygen in make-up water**. Table 8 separately reports **4, 8 and 16 ft s⁻¹** and **90, 170 and 697 days**. The directly matched **4-ft-s⁻¹, 697-day** column is transcribed below. The retrieved account does not establish the specimens’ product form or explicitly identify the rate calculation as weight loss. **Table 7 contains nominal composition limits, not measured analyses**, and its “Cu+Ag” entries cannot be read as 99.5 wt% copper *in addition to* the listed Ni or Al. (banning1973corrosionresistanceof pages 16-19, banning1973corrosionresistanceof pages 19-21)

| Material; Table 7 nominal composition, wt% | Table 8 corrosion rate: 4 ft s⁻¹, 697 days |
|---|---:|
| **C122**, phosphorus-deoxidized copper: Cu+Ag **≥99.9**, P **0.015–0.040** | **0.99 mpy** |
| **C608**, aluminum bronze: Al **5.0–6.5**, Fe **≤0.10** | **0.75 mpy** |
| **C613**, aluminum bronze: Al **6.0–8.0**, Fe **≤3.5**, Sn **0.2–0.5** | **0.73 mpy** |
| **C706**, 90–10 Cu–Ni: Ni **9–11**, Fe **1.0–1.8** | **0.70 mpy** |
| **C715**, 70–30 Cu–Ni: Ni **29–33**, Fe **0.4–0.7** | **0.46 mpy** |

All five numbers are from the **same Table 8 column**, rather than rates assembled from different tests. Table 7 is the source of the stated wt% *specifications*. (banning1973corrosionresistanceof pages 16-19, banning1973corrosionresistanceof pages 19-21, banning1973corrosionresistanceof media 97c8a396)

A further bronze comparison is **R. O. Lewis and F. LaQue (1981), *Evaluation of Copper-Nickel Alloys for OTEC Applications*, DOI: [10.2172/6255887](https://doi.org/10.2172/6255887), Table XIV**. This is a **DOE compilation of “Inco Unpublished Data.”** Its *uncoupled* specimens were exposed for **one year** in seawater flowing at **0.6 m s⁻¹**: aluminum bronze, **43.2 µm/y (1.7 mpy)**; C70600, **30.5 µm/y (1.2 mpy)**; C71500, **20.3 µm/y (0.8 mpy)**. Table XIV does **not** identify the aluminum-bronze grade or establish that it contains 5–9 wt% Al; nor does it give specimen form, temperature, measured compositions or an explicit mass-loss method. It is therefore a useful bronze/Cu–Ni comparison, but **not a verified Cu–5Al-to-Cu–9Al comparison**. These are the *uncoupled* rows, not the table’s galvanically coupled results. (lewis1981evaluationofcoppernickel pages 48-55, lewis1981evaluationofcoppernickel media 84e4a13c)

## Scope and remaining gap

An additional **peer-reviewed, weight-loss** Cu–Ni comparison—but **without copper or bronze**—is **S. A. Al-Fozan and A. U. Malik (2008), *Desalination* 228:61–67, DOI: [10.1016/j.desal.2007.08.007](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.desal.2007.08.007)**. Rectangular **50 × 20 × 2 mm** specimens were fully immersed in slowly moving (**12 L h⁻¹**) Arabian Gulf seawater at **25 ± 5°C**. **Table 1** gives measured compositions, wt%: 90/10 Cu–Ni **Cu 88.18, Ni 9.93, Fe 1.41, Mn 0.273**; 70/30 Cu–Ni **Cu 68.81, Ni 30, Fe 0.53, Mn 0.51**. In **Table 3**, fully submerged 90/10 specimens measured **0.145 mpy at 198 days** and **0.082 mpy at 401 days**; 70/30 specimens measured **0.067 mpy at 192 days** and **0.049 mpy at 365 days**. The exposure durations differ by alloy, so even these are **same-study, same-conditions results, not exact same-duration pairs**. (alfozan2008effectofseawater pages 3-5, alfozan2008effectofseawater pages 1-3)

**No verified same-test numerical series containing intermediate Cu–2Ni or Cu–5Ni alongside Cu–10Ni and Cu–30Ni was located.** Ravindran and the Cohen–Whitted compilation supply the narrower **Cu/10Ni/30Ni** progression, with the composition and method qualifications above. Neither a Cu–Ni-only quiet-water table nor a polarization curve has been substituted for the requested copper-versus-Cu–Ni mass-loss evidence. (ravindran1983coppernickelalloysfor pages 5-7, banning1973corrosionresistanceof pages 16-19, banning1973corrosionresistanceof pages 19-21)

info.query: I need SAME-TEST seawater corrosion data that compare unalloyed copper (or a copper alloy with less than 5 wt% Ni) against 90-10 copper-nickel (C70600) and/or 70-30 copper-nickel (C71500), measured in the same study under the same conditions (natural or synthetic seawater, or 3.5 wt% NaCl; quiet immersion preferred; mass loss or weight loss preferred over Tafel; 30 days or longer preferred). Also any same-study series of Cu-Ni alloys with several Ni contents between 0 and 30 wt% (for example Cu-2Ni, Cu-5Ni, Cu-10Ni, Cu-30Ni), and any same-study comparison of an aluminum bronze (Cu-5Al to Cu-9Al, with or without Fe) against a copper-nickel. For each, give: the paper (authors, year, DOI), each alloy's composition in wt%, product form, the test (medium, temperature, flow, duration, method), and each alloy's corrosion rate exactly as reported with units. List only numbers you can see in the source; say which table or figure each comes from. Prefer peer-reviewed papers and authoritative compilations (for example LaQue, Efird, the Copper Development Association, INCO/Nickel Institute), and say which are compilations.
